closing_reflection: Perhaps viability is not a switch that settles when abortion becomes permissible. It may instead change which ways of ending a pregnancy are possible. But if the law protects life by compelling another person to sustain it, what values are we choosing—and can we justify them?

slides.headline: When should abortion be legal?
slides.body: A question about viability becomes a question about dependence, bodily autonomy, and what the law can compel.

slides.headline: Viability seemed like a defensible boundary.
slides.body:
A fetus is biologically alive before it could survive outside the womb. But legal protection and biological life are not identical questions.

I began by thinking the law could permit abortion until survival outside the womb became possible.
slides.alt: Viability seemed like a defensible boundary.

slides.headline: Does dependence make a life less protected?
slides.body:
A person on a ventilator might die without it. We would not take that dependence as permission to kill them.

If viability is doing the moral work, why does that analogy feel so troubling?
slides.alt: Does dependence make a life less protected?

slides.headline: A ventilator is not a womb.
slides.body:
A ventilator is a machine. A pregnancy is sustained inside the body of another living person.

Does a right to life also create a right to the use of someone else’s body? Can the law compel the pregnancy to continue?
slides.alt: A ventilator is not a womb.

slides.headline: But care does not end at birth.
slides.body:
A newborn cannot survive without other people’s time, resources, and attention. Society imposes obligations toward dependent children.

If dependence on another person is relevant, why does birth change the nature of the obligation?
slides.alt: But care does not end at birth.

slides.headline: Minutes before. Minutes after.
slides.body:
Imagine the same child immediately before and after delivery. We treat killing a newborn differently from ending a pregnancy.

Is the difference simply location? Or is there a principled difference between refusing bodily support and ending another life?

slides.headline: Ending pregnancy need not mean ending fetal life.
slides.body:
Where delivery is medically possible, a pregnancy can sometimes end while the child survives. That does not make delivery risk-free, nor every option available in every case.

But it changes what the law might be trying to permit or prohibit.
slides.alt: Ending pregnancy need not mean ending fetal life.

slides.headline: Which values are hiding inside the rule?
slides.body:
Nietzsche did not give us an answer to abortion law. His challenge to inherited moral certainty offers a way to examine our assumptions.

What counts as affirming life here—and whose life, freedom, and burden have we placed in the frame?
slides.alt: Which values are hiding inside the rule?

slides.headline: Viability may change the options, not settle the ethics.
slides.body:
It still matters whether survival outside the womb is possible. But that fact cannot, by itself, decide what one person must endure for another.

Perhaps the legal boundary should ask not only when survival is possible, but what ending a pregnancy entails.
slides.alt: Viability may change the options, not settle the ethics.
